title: CauKer: Time Series Models Trained on Synthetic Data
one_liner: Instead of spending weeks collecting and curating real time series for training, generate fake ones that are cheap and still teach the model to work on real data.
lead: A time series foundation model (a large model trained to read sequences of numbers over time) normally requires weeks of work collecting and cleaning real-world data before it can be trained. This paper introduces CauKer, a tool that generates diverse fake time series data that looks realistic—with trends, seasonal patterns, and complex relationships—and can pretrain these models just as well as real data, but at a fraction of the cost and time. It works by combining two ideas: Gaussian Process kernels (a method to build realistic patterns by mixing trends, cycles, and noise) and Structural Causal Models (a way to encode how one number in a sequence causally influences another over time).

paras: A time series foundation model is a large machine-learning model trained to understand sequences—like stock prices, sensor readings, or weather data—that unfold over time. Before such a model can work on real data, it must be trained on a huge collection of examples, usually hand-picked and cleaned from real-world sources. Collecting and curating this data takes months and costs hundreds of thousands of dollars.

A naive approach: just grab raw real-world sequences and train on them. This breaks because real data is expensive to obtain, noisy, and often lacks the systematic variety the model needs to learn general patterns. You end up training slowly and inefficiently, needing far more examples than you should.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: CauKer generates synthetic time series that look realistic and causally coherent, so you can pretrain the model on cheap fake data instead of expensive real data.

steps.text: User specifies how time-series components causally influence each other.
CauKer mixes standard patterns (trend, seasonality, noise) to build realistic individual sequences.
The Structural Causal Model ensures one sequence causally affects another in realistic ways.
Sample repeatedly from these combined patterns to create thousands of varied synthetic sequences.
Train the foundation model on synthetic data; it learns patterns that transfer to real sequences.

paras: CauKer changes the data itself—specifically, what training examples are fed into the foundation model. Instead of using real-world sequences collected by humans, it uses computationally generated synthetic sequences. The generation process is controlled: the user can specify causal relationships and diversity constraints, ensuring the fake data has realistic structure.

hidden.name: Causal structure preservation
paras: The hidden quantity CauKer measures is how faithfully the generated synthetic data preserves the causal relationships specified by a human. Causal coherence means: if the user says signal A causally drives signal B, then changes in A should reliably precede and explain changes in B in the synthetic data. A signal with low causal coherence has artificial patterns that do not reflect real cause-and-effect.

The paper estimates this by embedding a Structural Causal Model (a graph describing which signal causes which) into the Gaussian Process kernels, so that when data is sampled, the causal relationships automatically flow through. This is checked by verifying that learned models trained on the synthetic data generalize to real sequences—if causal structure is wrong, generalization fails.

heat.caption: Darker cells have stronger causal structure and are more critical to realism.

reads.html: If your goal is to make a fake time-series dataset that looks real and has believable cause-and-effect patterns, you need to make sure that when you change one signal, the others change in the expected way. That is causal coherence.

CauKer uses Structural Causal Models embedded in Gaussian Process kernels to generate synthetic sequences where causal relationships between signals are built in by design. This works because a model learns patterns from data—if the synthetic data encodes the right causal structure, the model learns those patterns and can apply them to real data with the same causal structure.

mechanism.h2: Why combining kernels and causal models works
paras: A Gaussian Process kernel is a mathematical tool that generates smooth, realistic patterns—like an upward trend, a repeating seasonal cycle, or noise that clusters in time. Alone, a kernel produces a single signal. To make a single time series feel real, you mix several kernels: one for the main trend, one for seasonality, one for random noise. This is step one.

Structural Causal Models add the second dimension: they encode which signal causally influences which. If you say signal B depends on signal A with a 5-step delay, the SCM bakes that relationship into the data generation. The trick is composing the kernels according to the SCM: when you sample signal A, that sample determines signal B's kernel parameters, so B actually depends on A. Result: a synthetic dataset where causal relationships are embedded, not accidental.

This works because models learn patterns from data. If the synthetic data has realistic trends, seasonality, and true causal relationships, a model trained on it learns those patterns. When the model encounters real data—which has the same kinds of trends and causal relationships—the learned patterns transfer. The model does not overfit to noise or artifacts because the synthetic data was built to avoid them.

stages.s: Define kernels for trend, seasonality, noise
Compose kernels according to causal graph
Sample from composed kernels many times
Diverse synthetic time series with causal structure

math.words: The total synthetic sequence is built by adding kernel components weighted by their importance. If a kernel captures trend, it gets a high weight; if it captures rare noise, it gets a low weight. The weights are set so that causally upstream signals influence downstream signals.
math.equation: y_t = w_trend * k_trend(t) + w_season * k_season(t) + w_noise * epsilon_t + sum_j w_j * f_j(x_j, t - delay_j)
symbols: The synthetic value at time step t
Weight for the trend component, typically high
The trend kernel evaluated at time t, e.g., a slow upward curve
The seasonal kernel, e.g., a repeating sine wave
Weight for random noise, typically low
Random noise at time t, drawn from a normal distribution
Weight for causal influence from signal j
Function mapping signal j's past value to influence on current signal, with delay
How many time steps signal j lags before affecting current signal

charts.title: Old way: real data only
charts.note: Collecting and curating real data is slow and expensive, and models may overfit.

charts.title: CauKer way: synthetic pretraining
charts.note: Synthetic data is instant to generate because it is computed, not manually collected. Models pretrained on it generalize better because they have already learned realistic patterns before seeing real data, and the synthetic causal structure matches real data. Total cost drops because the time-consuming collection and curation steps vanish.

items.html: If the causal graph is wrong (e.g., you say B depends on A when actually A depends on B), the synthetic data will encode nonsense. The model learns invalid patterns and fails on real data.

If the trend or seasonal kernels do not reflect the real data's actual ranges or cycles, the synthetic sequences stay artificial. A kernel that produces only trends between 10-20 when real data spans 0-100 creates a mismatch.
If the generator only produces sequences that look alike (e.g., all have the same trend slope), the model underfits; it has not seen enough variety to generalize.
Real time series often have lag: a stock price drop today affects trading volume tomorrow. If CauKer does not encode these delays correctly, causal relationships break down.

Specify the causal graph truthfully, set kernel ranges to match real data bounds, ensure the generator samples diverse combinations, and validate that models pretrained on the synthetic data transfer well to held-out real sequences.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A minimal demo should: (1) Define a simple three-signal causal structure (signal A is a root cause, signal B depends on A with a 2-step lag, signal C depends on B); (2) Use CauKer to generate 10,000 synthetic time series following that structure; (3) Train a small time-series classifier (e.g., a model with 100,000 parameters) to classify the synthetic data (e.g., high vs low trend); (4) Test that trained model on a held-out set of real time-series data (e.g., from a public benchmark like UCR time-series archive); (5) Measure classification accuracy. The demo must show that accuracy on real test data is higher than a baseline model trained on a smaller amount of real data, proving that synthetic pretraining transfers.
demo.closing: The demo is not complete unless it proves that a model pretrained on CauKer synthetic data outperforms a model trained from scratch on real data alone. This is essential because if pretraining on synthetic data does not improve accuracy or if it only works on particular datasets, the claim that synthetic pretraining transfers collapses.
